cases.statement: For an idempotent linear endomorphism p, each vector has a unique decomposition as a vector in range p plus a vector in kernel p.
assumptions: K is a field; V is a K-module with an additive commutative group.
p is linear and p composed with p equals p.
proof_outline: Take u=p(x) and v=x-p(x).
Idempotence implies p(v)=0; u lies in the range by construction.
For any competing decomposition x=p(z)+v with p(v)=0, applying p identifies p(z)=p(x).
Subtract the common range component to identify the kernel component.

hard_negative.statement: The decomposition exists for every endomorphism, without idempotence.
hard_negative.counterexample: On Q^2 set p(a,b)=(b,0). Its range and kernel both equal the first coordinate axis, so x=(0,1) has no such decomposition.

cases.statement: A continuous strictly increasing function on [a,b] with negative and positive endpoint values has exactly one zero in [a,b].
assumptions: a and b are real with a<=b.
f is continuous on the closed interval and strictly increasing there.
proof_outline: The endpoint inequalities put zero between f(a) and f(b).
Apply the intermediate value theorem to obtain an interval point with value zero.
Strict monotonicity on the interval implies injectivity there.
Compare an arbitrary other interval zero with the constructed point to prove uniqueness.

hard_negative.statement: Continuity and endpoint sign change alone imply a unique zero.
hard_negative.counterexample: f(x)=x^3-x on [-2,2] is continuous, changes endpoint signs, and vanishes at -1,0,1. Counterexamples.lean proves these facts.

cases.statement: If P is a prime ideal and I intersection J is contained in P, then I is contained in P or J is contained in P.
assumptions: R is a commutative ring.
I, J, P are ideals of R; P is prime.
I intersection J is contained in P.
proof_outline: Assume neither ideal is contained in P.
Choose x in I outside P and y in J outside P.
Ideal absorption puts xy in both I and J, hence in P.
Primality forces x or y into P, contradicting their choices.

hard_negative.statement: The conclusion holds for an arbitrary proper ideal P.
hard_negative.counterexample: In Z take I=(2), J=(3), P=(6). I intersection J=P, but neither I nor J is contained in P.

cases.statement: A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space has a continuous two-sided inverse.
assumptions: X and Y are topological spaces.
X is compact and Y is Hausdorff.
f:X->Y is continuous and bijective.
proof_outline: Each closed subset of compact X is compact.
Its continuous image is compact, hence closed in Hausdorff Y.
Thus f is a closed continuous bijection, giving a homeomorphism.
The inverse equivalence is continuous and satisfies both inverse laws.

hard_negative.statement: The inverse remains continuous if compactness is omitted.
hard_negative.counterexample: The usual-angle map t -> exp(i*t) from [0,2pi) to the unit circle is a continuous bijection; its inverse is discontinuous at 1. The half-open interval is not compact.

cases.statement: Two horizontally adjacent commuting squares have a commuting outer rectangle.
assumptions: C is a category with six objects and the seven well-typed morphisms named in the Lean target.
The left and the right squares each commute.
proof_outline: Reassociate the outer top composite.
Use the right-square equality to replace its top-right route.
Reassociate and use the left-square equality.
Reassociate the bottom route to obtain the outer-square equality.

hard_negative.statement: The outer rectangle commutes when only the left square commutes.
hard_negative.counterexample: In the category of sets take every object to be a singleton except the final object {0,1}. All maps between singletons are unique; choose final right arrow constant 1 and final bottom arrow constant 0. The left square commutes and the outer rectangle does not.

cases.statement: For nonzero complex z, z+1/z is real exactly when z is real or its norm-square equals one.
assumptions: z is a nonzero complex number.
Real means the imaginary component vanishes; norm-square is Complex.normSq.
proof_outline: Nonzero z gives nonzero norm-square.
Express the imaginary part of z+1/z as im(z)-im(z)/normSq(z).
Clear the nonzero denominator and factor im(z)*(normSq(z)-1).
Use the zero-product property and check each converse branch.

hard_negative.statement: For nonzero z, z+1/z is real only when z is real.
hard_negative.counterexample: z=i is not real, but z+1/z=0 since normSq(i)=1. This algebraic family is not itself complex-analysis breadth.

cases.statement: An entire complex-valued function whose norm has a uniform positive lower bound is constant.
assumptions: f:C->C is complex differentiable everywhere.
eps is a positive real number.
eps <= norm(f(z)) for every complex z.
proof_outline: The positive lower bound makes f nowhere zero.
The reciprocal 1/f is entire by the differentiation rule for inverses.
Its norm is bounded by 1/eps, using the norm-inverse identity and reversed reciprocal inequality.
Apply Liouville to the reciprocal and use injectivity of inversion to deduce f(z)=f(0).

hard_negative.statement: A continuous function with a uniform positive norm lower bound must be constant.
hard_negative.counterexample: f(z)=1+norm(z), embedded in C, is continuous with norm at least one, and f(0)=1 while f(1)=2. Counterexamples.lean proves the bound and nonconstancy; it does not claim complex differentiability.

cases.statement: The polynomial x^3-x supplies distinct zeros despite continuity and endpoint sign change on [-2,2].
assumptions: The domain and codomain are real.
No monotonicity assumption is made.
proof_outline: Use the polynomial x^3-x.
Polynomial continuity follows from continuous arithmetic.
Evaluate endpoints and zeros -1,0,1 exactly.
Exhibit -1 different from 1 to refute uniqueness.

hard_negative.statement: The three roots collapse to a unique root.
hard_negative.counterexample: The exact distinct values -1 and 1 both give zero.

cases.statement: The function z -> 1+norm(z) has norm at least one everywhere and is not constant.
assumptions: The real-valued norm is embedded in C.
The claim is a lower bound and a nonconstancy witness, not holomorphicity.
proof_outline: Rewrite the function as an embedded nonnegative real.
Its complex norm is the absolute value of that real.
Nonnegativity removes the absolute value.
Evaluate at zero and one to show different values.

hard_negative.statement: A positive lower norm bound suffices for Liouville without complex differentiability.
hard_negative.counterexample: The displayed function gives values 1 and 2.

cases.statement: For c>0 and real t, classify when x^3-3x+t has three distinct real roots alpha<beta<gamma and c+alpha,c+beta,c+gamma are sides of a nondegenerate triangle.
assumptions: c>0 and t is real.
All three roots must be real and pairwise distinct.
Triangle side lengths must be positive and satisfy strict triangle inequalities.
proof_outline: Differentiate to locate extrema at -1 and 1; three distinct roots occur exactly for -2<t<2.
Locate roots in (-2,-1),(-1,1),(1,2) and use Vieta alpha+beta+gamma=0.
Triangle feasibility reduces to c>2*gamma; hence c<=2 is impossible.
For 2<c<4 monotonicity of x^3-3x on (1,infinity) gives 3*c/2-c^3/8<t<2.
For c>=4 every -2<t<2 works; check all strict boundaries separately.

hard_negative.statement: Allow equality in the triangle inequality while keeping the same strict parameter range.
hard_negative.counterexample: c=3,t=9/8 has gamma=3/2 and alpha,beta=(-3 plus/minus sqrt(21))/4. The two shorter lengths sum exactly to the longest.

cases.method_constraints: Use only high-school mathematics; finite or numerical checks alone cannot prove classification.

cases.statement: Classify all positive integer pairs (a,b) with a^2+b^2+1=3ab.
assumptions: a and b are positive integers.
The coefficient is exactly 3 and the additive constant is exactly 1.
proof_outline: Order a<=b; if a=1 then b is 1 or 2.
For a>1 define bprime=3*a-b; the equation gives b*bprime=a^2+1, so bprime>0.
The identity (b-a)*(b-2*a)=a^2-1>0 forces b>2*a, hence bprime<a.
Substitution gives the smaller solution (bprime,a); well-ordering reduces to the base cases.
Reverse descent: u0=u1=1 and u(n+2)=3*u(n+1)-u(n); all solutions are adjacent terms in either order.
Prove recurrence positivity and the preserved equation inductively to establish sufficiency and completeness.

hard_negative.statement: Drop positivity but keep the positive-sequence classification.
hard_negative.counterexample: (-1,-1) satisfies the same equation and is outside the proposed positive sequence.

cases.statement: Uniformly order n red and n blue balls (n>=1), conditioned on every prefix having red>=blue. If K is half the first positive tie time and T counts positive ties including the final tie, prove P(K=k)=C(k-1)*C(n-k)/C(n) and E[T]=3*n/(n+2).
assumptions: Every color word is equally likely before conditioning.
Every prefix has at least as many red as blue balls.
C(m)=binomial(2*m,m)/(m+1); 1<=k<=n.
T includes the final tie and excludes time zero.
proof_outline: Use reflection to count admissible balanced words by C(n).
First return at time 2k removes an outer red/blue pair and leaves independent admissible words of sizes k-1 and n-k.
Divide their product count by C(n) for the first-return distribution.
For the tie indicator at time 2j count C(j)*C(n-j) words.
Sum the indicators and use the Catalan convolution to get (C(n+1)-C(n))/C(n).
Evaluate the ratio of Catalan numbers to obtain 3*n/(n+2).

hard_negative.statement: Remove the prefix condition and retain the same expectation.
hard_negative.counterexample: For n=2 the six unconditioned color words have mean positive tie count 5/3, whereas the conditioned formula is 3/2.

cases.statement: For a nondegenerate isosceles triangle ABC with AB=AC and midpoint M of BC, prove AM perpendicular BC.
assumptions: A,B,C form a nondegenerate triangle.
AB=AC; M is the midpoint of BC.
Any supplied figure must be transcribed and confirmed without using display coordinates as premises.
proof_outline: T2 must supply checked instantiated geometric steps and a Lean source/trace binding.
T2 must record foundational assumptions and transitive axioms.
T3 must render the matching geometry inline with TikZ source and persistence.
T2/T3 must check degenerate and inconsistent-input cases through the actual integration.

hard_negative.statement: Remove nondegeneracy and still infer a unique perpendicular line AM.
hard_negative.counterexample: Take B=(-1,0), C=(1,0), A=M=(0,0). AB=AC and M is the midpoint, but A and M do not determine a line.

integration_obligations: MRD-004 actual inline figure and TikZ
